ar_lutz_cave.blurb: A steep, overhanging cave on Webber Mountain (also known as East Mountain) near Springdale in northwest Arkansas. Bouldering makes up most of the 29 climbs, with problems ranging from a very easy start through the middle V grades to a few very hard lines at the top end. About a dozen sport routes, from the mid 5.x range up to 5.12, and a lone trad line round things out. Most of it was developed in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and the cave is the region's best-known piece of roof and cave bouldering. The walk from the road is short, about five minutes uphill on an old road.

ar_hudson_mountain.blurb: A sandstone crag near the village of Cowell in the Ozarks of north-central Arkansas, and one of the busiest sport venues in the Cowell area. Almost all of its 28 climbs are bolted sport lines, with a few trad routes including a well-known crack. Grades run from 5.7 to low 5.13, but the bulk sits between 5.10 and 5.12, so strong intermediates are well served and there are a few easier warm-ups. The rock is good for the region, and the cliff has steep walls, big caves and amphitheaters with wide views. The approach is short, and the crag lies on the way to neighbouring walls such as Invasion Wall.

ar_cellar_the.blurb: A compact bouldering circuit in the Gasfields, a patch of pine woods in the central Arkansas foothills not far from Little Rock. Its 28 problems sit on fine-grained sandstone and favour slopers and compression over crimps, with a Font-like feel. Most lines fall between V2 and V4, with a harder tail reaching V8 or V9, including the region's well-known hard problem Darcy's Law. The boulders sit in small garden-like clusters, and a cave gives shade most of the day, though winter brings sun. Few people have climbed here in recent years, so expect to do some brushing. It works better as a local training spot than a destination for travelers.

ar_wall_of_moderates_the.blurb: The first wall on the left as you reach the cliff line at Stack Rock, a remote sandstone crag in the Richland Creek area of north-central Arkansas. Of its 28 climbs, about three quarters are trad lines that take gear in horizontal cracks, with the rest bolted sport routes; many lines have since been given bolted anchors. Grades run from 5.4 to 5.10, with most between 5.4 and 5.8, which makes it a gentle place to learn or to warm up. The hike from the parking area takes roughly twenty minutes and is longer than most in Arkansas. Summer growth gets thick, so cooler months suit it best.

ar_hood_the.blurb: A small, quiet zone within the Cowell area of Newton County in north-central Arkansas, just up the road from Hudson Mountain. Most of its 27 climbs are bolted sport lines, with the weight on 5.10 through 5.12 and a good number of 5.11s and 5.12s, plus one much harder line beyond that. Around half a dozen boulder problems add variety, running from V2 up to V9. Only a few routes are easy, so this suits experienced climbers. The approach is about three minutes on a trail, with the roped climbing to the right and the boulders to the left. Development here is recent and still ongoing.

ar_tomb_the.blurb: The signature wall at Rock Creek, a secluded sport area in the Big Piney region of north-central Arkansas. The cliff is steep and about 80 feet tall, with large birch trees below and a seasonal waterfall beside it. Nearly all of its 27 climbs are bolted sport lines, with just two trad routes. There is a single 5.9 and a single 5.10, then the bulk of the wall sits at 5.11 and 5.12, topped by a handful of 5.13s. Expect powerful, burly climbing that rewards a range of techniques; it is one of the best places in the state for hard sport climbing and not a spot for beginners.
